title: Cannabis Retail Outlets: What’s In A Name? What Is The Best Model?

content_html_sanitized:
Recently, The New York Times, carried an unusually competent bit of journalism about cannabis. Is the Local Weed Store the New Place to Hang Out?

 

“Young adults are drinking less alcohol and seeking more connection, and New York’s dispensaries are putting themselves out there as alternative gathering spaces.”

 

It explains, “From intimate classes to block parties, hosting events has given dispensaries in New York a way around rules limiting their ability to market their businesses. As many Americans choose to drink less alcohol and seek connection offline, the activities allow the sellers to offer places where people can gather. Dispensary owners also hope that some of the visitors will become customers and that the events will help their businesses gain acceptance among neighbors who might still hold negative views of cannabis.”

 

There are approximately 3,100 bars that serve alcohol in New York City. Thank goodness everyone agrees that alcohol is harmless!

 

There are also approximately 13,000 “bodegas”, corner convenience stores, that sell beer and cigarettes. Well known health supplements.

 

The number of legal “marijuana dispensaries” is increasing rapidly, but hundreds of unlicensed dispensaries remain.

 

Let’s start at the beginning. Why are they called “dispensaries”?

 

After Proposition 215 passed in 1996, when the people of California had the audacity to disregard their betters, and allow doctors to recommend (not prescribe!!!) “something called marihuana” the appropriate term really was “dispensary”, a place where medications were dispensed.

 

The term is now being used in New York and elsewhere to mean a store specializing in selling recreational cannabis. Certainly, it should remind us how it all began and that the Prohibitionists still deny that cannabis has any medical value.

 

Meanwhile, back in Amsterdam, fifty years ago, it was easy to get a license to open a “coffee shop”, so when Henk DeVries wanted to open a cannabis retail business, the Bull Dog, he called it a coffee shop. And they really do sell coffee.

 

In Las Vegas, when they recognized that there was no place to smoke all that legal weed, they decided to call them “cannabis consumption lounges”, but made them extraordinarily difficult to actually open.

See It’s Time for Las Vegas to Reinvent Itself Again. This Time as the Newest Amsterdam.

 

In Barcelona, when the (over)tourism boom got started about 15 years ago, they found a loophole by calling them “Cannabis Social Clubs”. The Spanish government doesn’t like the idea, so they are much more discreet today, and not really “social clubs”, but “tolerated” in most major cities.

 

When the German parliament wanted to take cannabis out of the black market, they couldn’t get a majority for actual retail outlets like the ones in The Netherlands, a short walk across the border, so they voted for real social clubs, which are great but will not kill the black market.

 

Of course, there is an amusing precedent for the use of a euphemism for alcohol retailers, “package stores”, but, they are definitely for off premise consumption.

 

Meanwhile, there is not a single model for cannabis legalization.

 

There can be real medical dispensaries or special pharmacies for patients who need knowledgeable “bud tenders”, bodegas or convenience stores for packaged pre rolled joints, social clubs that may actually be coops for gardeners, the equivalent of nightclubs and restaurants, but with weed instead of alcohol, and of course good old Dutch style “Coffee Shops”, where you can smoke and have a cup of coffee or tea, or maybe someday even iced tea in Texas. (It’s a libertarian thing.)

 

Meanwhile, what is the model I think we may need most?

The original London Coffee Houses, political venues where people can gather to discuss the issues of the day, especially how we end cannabis prohibition and make caffeine and cannabinoids the social lubricants that play a positive role in restoring our severely dysfunctional public discourse.
